title: Let out of jail, free to stalk: [Ontario Edition]
article: In a Scarborough courtroom, on a Friday morning just over two weeks ago, Peter Francis stood before a justice of the peace to convince the court why he should be released.

He had just spent seven days in jail, charged with criminal harassment- stalking- and uttering death threats against his estranged wife, Rayness. Francis was no stranger to the justice system: He had a conviction in 1989 for assault and possession of a weapon and there were some old allegations of sexual assault and sexual interference still before the courts.

Twelve days after his last court appearance, Francis would be dead, killed by police after he got a weapon, and shot his wife in the leg. The assault adds a fresh chapter to the continuing history of men accused of domestic violence being allowed out of jail- and going on to stalk their partners.

To bolster his chances of being released on bail, Francis had brought his cousin and a friend, Leroy Britton. Britton had actually met Francis through Rayness, who was a colleague of his at the Scarborough plant where they worked.

At the start of the hearing, Crown Attorney Dimitra Tsagaris outlined the reasons why Francis should be detained. She explained the couple had separated just a month ago after three years of marriage and that Rayness Francis was frightened of her husband and questioned his "mental stability."

She explained to the court that just a couple of weeks prior, Francis went to his wife's new residence and asked for some documentation concerning his car. Frightened, Rayness Francis contacted police. Tsagaris said Francis then retorted: "You better give me my stuff, or else when I'm finished with her she won't need her belongings."

Terrified, Rayness Francis asked family members to accompany her to and from work; she was worried her husband might try to attack. Those fears came true April 19, when Peter appeared as she drove to work with her 16-year-old nephew in the car and two other relatives in vehicles nearby. He pulled alongside her car, shouting, trying to get her to pull off the road.

Rayness called the police on her cellphone. Peter kept chasing her car, eventually forcing her off the road. Her windows were rolled up and the doors were locked, but she heard Peter shout: "You should be dead."
Then the police arrived, and Peter Francis was arrested. These allegations were presented at the April 26 bail hearing. With Britton and his cousin as his sureties, the 34-year-old was released.

Justice of the Peace James Allen said Francis was not allowed to drive, "communicate directly or indirectly with Rayness Francis; not to be found within 500 metres of her home or place of work," and not allowed to possess weapons.
"I won't impose a curfew," Allen said. "He's a grown man."

On May 7, Francis drove to A.G. Simpson Co. on Progress Dr., parked his car in the lot, and shot his estranged wife in the leg. Minutes later, he called for Britton, who was working inside the plant at the time.
Britton said in an interview this week he was on his way to the parking lot, hoping he could convince Francis to lay down his weapon. He heard the shot as he approached the front glass doors.

Outside, an impatient Francis had wheeled around- rifle in hand- to face a heavily armed Toronto police officer. He was shot and killed. The province's Special Investigations Unit, which probes all serious injury or death involving police in Ontario, is examining the actions of the Toronto police officers involved.
Rayness Francis escaped from her husband with minor physical injuries, and is recuperating with relatives.

As women fleeing relationships where there is physical or emotional abuse are urged to do, Rayness Francis had told people about her fears. She had discussed getting a restraining order- and indeed, the justice of the peace ordered Peter Francis to stay away from her home and place of business- and that she was bothered that her estranged husband was showing up at the plant.

"The minute I heard it was a domestic, I thought, 'Jesus, it's Rayness,'" said a woman who knows Francis and the troubles she had been having with the man. "He was showing up at the workplace and the workplace had already told him he wasn't welcome."

Despite the terrifying event, Rayness Francis is alive- and she is one of the lucky ones, after a two-week period in which three Ontario men have been charged with killing women in domestic violence cases.

Cosimo Pasqualino, 46, was arrested and charged with second- degree murder after his spouse of 20 years, Marisa, 36, a mother of four, was found in her home with fatal gunshot wounds May 1. Pasqualino has been remanded in custody at Metro West Detention Centre until May 22.

Angus Snow of Orangeville was found in a Thunder Bay hotel and charged with first-degree murder in the death of his wife, Shirley. Shirley Snow was killed after being hit by a van in a crowded shopping mall parking lot last Sunday. Snow appeared in court Friday in Orangeville and was remanded until May 17. In Sarnia, after a stabbing death in a parking garage, former Commonwealth Games boxing champion, Jeremy Molitor, 24, was charged with first-degree murder. Molitor's ex-girlfriend, Jessica Nethery, 21, was found dead May 4. At the time, there were bail conditions ordering Molitor to stay away from Nethery, pending an assault trial.

The issue of violent men killing partners after being allowed out of jail is one that's been addressed in courts and inquests more than once, said Pamela Cross, legal co-ordinator for the Ontario Women's Justice Network.

The juries probing the deaths of Gillian Hadley (shot to death June 20, 2000 by her husband, who had violated court orders to stay away from her) and Arlene May (killed in 1996 by her ex-boyfriend) both confronted the issue of men being allowed out on bail, but it's a problem that's still not solved. Every year in Ontario, about 40 women are killed by their domestic partners.
"I hate saying, "What would be the three things that most would save women?'" Cross said. "I do it, nonetheless, in my own head. Bail, number one. Bail, number two. Bail, number three.
"It's a huge problem."

The Hadley jury thought so, too: It dedicated nine of its 53 recommendations to the issue of bail. And jurors pointed out in the preamble to their recommendations that domestic violence is a crime with particular characteristics: "The likelihood of repeat violence is common and at most times predictable," they wrote. "The victim is known in advance."

The jury recommended the Criminal Code of Canada be amended to make bail hearings for those arrested for domestic violence "reverse onus," meaning the accused must show why they should not be detained; normally, it is up to the crown attorneys to show why someone should remain in custody. It also suggested any person accused of domestic violence who breaches conditions set out by the court be held in custody until their trial.
"I'm a lawyer, and from a civil liberties point of view, I have some big problems with it," Cross said of reverse onus bail hearings.
"But I also think that this is a serious enough problem that we may have to suspend some civil liberties for some individuals if it's the only way to keep victims safe."
